- If sentiment is consistently low (≤0.33) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast peaks and shift toward lower values.
- If sentiment is consistently high (≥0.67) and model shows sharp spikes, cap forecast at 1.5x recent average or 20% below peak to avoid overshoot.
- When history shows mean reversion (e.g., recent values trending down), model often overcorrects upward; dampen forecast slope and align with recent 5-day moving average.
- If sentiment alternates between high/low with no clear trend, model tends to overfit short-term noise; use 10-day smoothing or ignore sentiment-driven extremes.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true values are consistently below 1.5x recent 18-day average, model is overconfident; apply 30% downward bias unless sentiment strongly supports upside.
- If sentiment history shows increasing negativity (e.g., 3+ consecutive 0.00 or 0.33), model often fails to adjust downward; apply 20–40% downward correction to avoid “sentiment lag” error.
- When model forecasts spike after a low sentiment period, true values often lag — apply 1–2 day delay correction or reduce peak by 50% if sentiment remains negative.
- If sentiment is high but model forecasts are low, model may be underestimating sentiment-driven momentum — increase forecast by 15–30% if sentiment >0.67 and recent history is stable.
